title: Microburst queue occupancy and preemption tradeoffs
content:
Summary:

Short: a set of experiments to understand how short, high-arrival-rate microbursts interact with our continuous batching scheduler, and how preemption and per-priority queue caps affect P50/P95/P99 tail behavior. We observed that modest microbursts (100-400 qps for ~200ms) create queue-occupancy spikes that cause P99 to jump 3-5x despite stable average throughput.

Motivation / Context:
- Customer incidents show transient failures and large 99th percentile latency increases during short traffic spikes even when average load is below capacity.
- We suspect interactions between: admission queuing, batch formation waiting timeout, fairness logic that rebalances from long-waiting streams, and preemption heuristics that flush batches early.

Hypotheses we tested:
1) Large max_batch_size + long max_wait_ms amplifies microburst impact: a small burst fills a single large batch and delays others waiting for kernel launch.
2) Preemption (early flush of an in-flight batch to honor latency SLOs) can either help or hurt: it reduces waiting time for the burst but can increase kernel launch overhead and reduce throughput, worsening tails for other requests.
3) Per-priority queue caps and admission shaping mitigate tail spikes by bounding queue occupancy.

Experimental setup (hardware/software):
- GPU: single NVIDIA A40 (simulated multi-tenant on same node by multiple worker processes).
- Runtime binary: rti-server v1.14.2 (instrumentation branch).
- Model: open-gpt-small (approx 1.7B) with typical kv-cache enabled; token generation to 128 tokens.
- Config knobs under test: max_batch_size (32,64,128), max_wait_ms (2,8,20), preemption: {off, early-flush-threshold-ms=5, aggressive}, per-priority-queue-cap (none, 16, 32).
- Workloads: background steady poisson at 60 qps; microburst: square pulse for 200ms at 300 qps added to background. Also tested Poisson bursts and heavy-tailed interarrival.
- Metrics captured: enqueued_length_over_time, batch_size_histogram, kernel_launch_rate, req_latency_ms (p50,p95,p99), CPU scheduler idle, CUDA stream utilization, context-switches, per-worker queue lengths.

Key commands / measurement notes:
- traffic generator: python loadgen.py --target 60 --burst 300 --burst-length-ms 200 --arrival-pattern square
- runtime tracing: ./rti-server --trace=queue,profiler --trace-out /tmp/trace.pb
- extracted queue occupancy: go run tools/trace_processor.go --metric=queue_len /tmp/trace.pb

Results (selected):
- Baseline (max_batch_size=128, max_wait_ms=20, preemption=off, no queue caps):
  - P50: 28 ms, P95: 72 ms, P99: 415 ms during burst windows.
  - Batch-size median: 92, batch-size 95th: 126 (so kernel runs are large but infrequent).
  - Queue occupancy spikes to 240 requests queued (across worker shards) during 200ms microburst.

- Small batch / short-wait (max_batch_size=32, max_wait_ms=2, preemption=off):
  - P50: 22 ms, P95: 56 ms, P99: 128 ms (dramatic improvement at the 99th).
  - Kernel launch rate increased x3; throughput sustained but GPU kernel overhead rose ~12% (measured by CUDA kernel-time / wall-time).
  - Observed drop in average batch efficiency but tail improved.

- Aggressive preemption (baseline batch sizes, preemption=aggressive):
  - P50 similar to baseline, P95 slightly worse (+6ms), P99 variable: sometimes reduced to ~220ms, sometimes increased to ~520ms depending on burst timing.
  - Root cause: preemption causes partially-filled batches to be flushed which increases kernel-launch frequency; when bursts overlap across shards it triggers many near-simultaneous launches causing GPU scheduling contention.

- Per-priority queue cap (cap=32 for low-priority traffic; background low-priority 60 qps):
  - Tail for high-priority requests improved (P99 reduced ~25%) because caps prevented low-priority backlog from consuming queue slots during bursts.
  - However, capped requests saw immediate rejections or 429-like responses for some flows — acceptable for best-effort workloads but not for everyone.

Profiling / Evidence:
- Flamegraph of rti-server main thread: during bursts, ~45% of CPU time spent in queue management and serialization (packing tensor batches).
- CUDA timelines: many short kernels launched back-to-back with gaps: kernel-launch overhead ~0.6ms per kernel in our setup; when launch rate >100/s we see throughput inefficiencies.
- KV cache eviction logs: occasional thrash when many concurrent requests have different prefixes — increased memcpys. This correlated with a subset of high-latency outliers.

Interpretation / Root causes:
1) Large batches + long wait create opportunistic pooling that is good for throughput but fragile when bursty arrivals occur — a large batch formed by the burst delays other requests that then wait for the next kernel.
2) Preemption trades waiting latency for kernel-launch overhead; without limit it can amplify GPU contention under multi-shard concurrency.
3) Unbounded queue occupancy allows low-priority traffic to crowd out capacity during bursts, producing long tails for higher-priority requests.
4) Kernel-launch overhead and per-request serialization are non-negligible at high kernel rates and become the dominant inefficiency when we reduce batch sizes too far.

Mitigation options explored and recommended tradeoffs:
- Conservative: Reduce max_wait_ms to 8ms and cap max_batch_size to 64. Effect: P99 reduced ~40% during microbursts while keeping kernel-launch overhead acceptable. Good default for mixed workloads.

- Aggressive tail-first: Enable preemption with a circuit-breaker: allow early flush only if current kernel-launch-rate < 60/s and target batch occupancy > 40%. This lowered worst-case tails in synthetic tests but requires an additional kernel-rate meter.

- Priority shaping: implement per-priority queue caps (32) + best-effort rejection for overflowed low-priority queues. This protects high-priority traffic but requires product decisions about acceptable rejection behavior.

- Batch coalescing background thread: add a small coalescer thread that merges very small batches within a 1-2ms window to reduce kernel-launch overhead when we target small waits. This recovered ~6-8% of throughput lost by small batch config in our experiments.

Experimental artifacts / raw numbers (CSV-like lines):
- config,max_wait_ms,max_batch_size,preemption,queue_cap,p50,p95,p99,kernels/s
- baseline,20,128,off,none,28,72,415,18
- smallwait,2,32,off,none,22,56,128,54
- preempt_aggr,20,128,aggressive,none,30,78,520,36
- cap32,20,128,off,32,27,65,310,20
- smallwait_coalescer,2,32,off,none,24,60,134,40

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How does multi-GPU (multiple workers sharing PCIe) change kernel launch contention behavior? Need a follow-up run on 4xA40 with networked shards.
- Impact on quantized kernels (int8) where kernel-run time is shorter: does kernel-launch overhead dominate earlier? We should test similar configs with quantized models.
- User-visible behavior for capped queues: do we prefer soft-drop (delay + long-poll) vs immediate reject? Ops and Product need to align.

Immediate action items (owners):
- (Aisha) Roll default config in staging to max_wait_ms=8 and max_batch_size=64 for runtime-scheduler branch; monitor P99 for 72h. (ETA: one week).
- (Marcus) Implement kernel-launch-rate meter and proto circuit-breaker for preemption gating (PR created: linked). (ETA: 2 weeks).
- (Liu) Run multi-GPU microburst experiments and collect CUDA timelines across shards. (ETA: 2 weeks).
- (Diego / product) Decide acceptable behavior for queue caps (soft-reject vs immediate 429). (Sync meeting requested).

Notes and rough heuristics learned:
- Default: prefer shorter waits (5-10ms) for public API workloads with burstiness; longer waits can be defaults for highly stable enterprise reserved pools.
- Preemption should be rate-limited and aware of global kernel frequency to avoid thrashing.
- Per-priority caps are the most effective surgical fix for protecting SLOs but require product-level policy.

Appendix: quick grep snippets used for traces (for engineering reproducibility)
- extract occupancy: grep "queue_len" /tmp/trace.pb | python -m json.tool | awk '{print $2,$3}'
- kernel launches per sec: nvprof --events inst_executed /tmp/nvprof.out | python tools/parse_nvprof.py

End.
